title: Negative Feedback Effects Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 12
description:
Aarav's fest amplifier sounds perfect in the morning, gets quieter as the room heats up, and turns too loud when a new transistor goes in. How can an amplifier stay steady when its parts keep changing? With negative feedback: a trade where we give up some gain and get a steady gain, a wider bandwidth, less distortion and noise, and better input and output impedance.

On a live breadboard the open loop gain falls from 1000 to 500 as the amplifier heats up. Without feedback the output on the oscilloscope halves; with negative feedback (beta = 0.1) the gain only moves from 9.90 to 9.80, because A_f is almost 1/beta, set by two resistors. We derive gain stability (dA_f/A_f = (dA/A)/(1 + A beta), the desensitivity factor), watch the frequency response widen by (1 + A beta), see distortion and noise shrink, and compare input and output impedance for voltage series feedback. A worked example, the exam trap (bandwidth widens, it does not shrink), where it is asked, an original practice question with a full solution, and a formula card follow.

This is Episode 72 of PUC Electronics, Class 12, Chapter 4: Feedback in Amplifiers (Karnataka II PUC Electronics, voltage series negative feedback). Feedback amplifiers are not in the rationalised NCERT/CBSE Class 12 Physics book or the current ISC Physics syllabus, so this lesson follows the Karnataka PUC Electronics syllabus.
